edition: Issue 026: a poll where both sides lose but only one will admit it, the AI that renders you from memory, and KiwiSaver quietly beating Australia at something for once
tagline: Your 4-minute Tuesday reset. Zero fluff, maximum banter.

stories.headline: National bounces back into the 30s while Labour slumps to its 2023-defeat level in a new pre-vote poll
stories.summary: A 1News-Verian poll has National back into the 30s while Labour support has slid to around the level where it lost in 2023, just ahead of the start of early voting, with NZ First Opportunity revived as the potential kingmaker.

body.text: The latest 1News-Verian poll has National climbing back into the 30s while Labour support has slumped to roughly the level it was defeated at in 2023. The numbers land just ahead of the start of early voting, and put the tail of the party system back in the spotlight: Opportunity, the renamed NZ First vehicle, is positioned as the potential kingmaker again, having promised to negotiate with the largest party first. With both major parties short of what they want, the focus shifts to who can put a government together after the first votes are cast.

Ah, the pre-election poll ritual: two parties staring at the same numbers and both insisting the graph is on their side, like a couple arguing over which half of the bed they are comfortable on. National is back in the 30s, Labour is down to 2023 levels, and Opportunity is in the middle holding the pillow, promising to team up with whoever yells largest first. The poll is not telling us who wins, it is telling us who spends the next few weeks pretending a number that moves five points every Tuesday is a personality.

NZ Herald (Jamie Ensor, 20 Oct 2026) reporting the 1News-Verian poll: National has returned to the 30s, Labour support is down to around the level where the party was defeated at the 2023 election, ahead of the start of early voting. Opportunity, the NZ First-linked party, is the potential kingmaker and says it will negotiate with the largest party first.

stories.headline: The AI caricatures flooding your feed are ChatGPT drawing you from memory, and that is the privacy problem
stories.summary: Social feeds are filling with AI-generated caricatures made by uploading a selfie to ChatGPT, which renders a stylised scene from everything the model already knows about the person, delighting users but raising questions about how much personal data the trend normalises.

body.text: Your feed has been filling with charming, surreal illustrations of your friends and whanau: AI-generated caricatures. Users upload an image of themselves to ChatGPT and the model produces an animated, stylised picture drawing on everything it already knows about them, their hobbies, job, and other interests. The trend spreads fast because it is fun, easy to copy, and easy to share. But it has revived questions about privacy and what happens to the personal information people hand to AI software, and one expert warns the fun is quietly normalising how much personal data exists online.

Finally, an AI that has been keeping files on you for years and is now going to show its work in front of all your mates. Your lockdown hobbies, your job, that one festival you mention every time: it is all in there, rendered in cheerful cartoon form so you smile while it reads you out loud. The model knows exactly who you are, flattering right up until you remember that is only because you told it, unprompted, for months. It is the friend who brings up embarrassing stories at dinner, except this one knows your whole browser history and draws it in pastel.

RNZ (20 Oct 2026) reporting the ChatGPT caricature trend: users upload a selfie and the model generates an animated image based on everything it knows about the person. University of Waikato Professor of AI and Director of the AI Institute Albert Bifet said the trend risks normalising how much personal data exists online, adding that when something is cute or fun people stop asking hard questions. Featured users include makeup artist Tom Hovey and Ari Dayal.

stories.headline: KiwiSaver fees edge below Australias, but only if you are actually putting money in
stories.summary: New Deloitte research has KiwiSaver median fee just below Australia at 0.77 percent versus 0.79 percent despite our scheme running at a fraction of the scale, though it also notes 41 percent of members are not contributing and the average balance is only 40,340 dollars.

body.text: New research has New Zealand finally winning a comparison with Australia, and on the least glamorous ground possible: fees. Deloitte benchmarking found KiwiSaver median total fee was 0.77 percent to Australia 0.79 percent, despite our scheme running at a fraction of the scale of the Australian superannuation system, which is about 35 times larger with a 15-year head start. The UK is cheapest of the three at 0.32 percent. But the research is a reminder that low fees only help if money is going in: of KiwiSaver 3.44 million members, just over 2 million were contributing, 1.42 million (around 41 percent) classified as non-contributing, and the average balance was only about 40,340 dollars.

New Zealand has beaten Australia at something, and it is the international race to charge you the least for holding your retirement savings. Proper chest-thumping material. But here is the fine print that stops it being a clean victory lap: we win the fee race partly because only about 60 percent of members are actually putting anything in, and the average balance is roughly the price of a used hatchback. It is the fit person in the gym with the cheapest membership who never actually shows up. Low fees are great, but the money that stays in is the part doing the work.

NZ Herald and GoodReturns (Sep 2026), citing Deloitte research prepared for Generate: KiwiSaver median total fee of 0.77 percent was marginally below Australia 0.79 percent despite the Australian system being roughly 35 times larger; the UK was cheapest at 0.32 percent. Only 2.02 million of KiwiSaver 3.44 million members were contributing, the FMA classifying 1.42 million (41.3 percent) as non-contributing; the average balance rose 11 percent but was only 40,340 dollars. KiwiSaver default funds carried a median fee of 0.25 percent versus 0.85 percent for non-default options.

affiliate_cta.headline: Sizing up your money, your vote, or just an easier Tuesday? Here is where we would look.
affiliate_cta.body: From a poll that moves by five points every week, to the AI that has been quietly keeping notes on you, to a KiwiSaver fee you will finally not mind reading about: a nudge to sort the small stuff so the big stuff takes care of itself. No pitch, no pressure, just a calm look before you commit.
